title: What is a polygon?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton compares two ways to teach what he calls Category Atoms, concepts answered by a yes or no such as whether a shape is a polygon. A US colleague has students sort shapes freely, discuss their own rules, then infer the hidden polygon and non-polygon groups. Barton instead silently presents a deliberate sequence of examples and non-examples, changing one feature at a time, and then collects data from every student with thumbs up or down. He is careful not to claim his approach is better. He notes both defer the formal definition to the end and rely on non-examples, then closes with questions about speed, visible thinking, and enjoyment for teacher and students.
points: Concepts answered by yes or no, such as polygon or like terms, can be treated as Category Atoms, borrowing Kris Boulton's term.
The sorting-first approach lets students discover criteria, while Barton's example-sequence approach takes about 30 seconds and relies on carefully varied features.
Both approaches delay the abstract definition, since technical definitions carry little meaning for students.
Non-examples are central to conveying meaning in both, and Barton regrets not appreciating this for his first twelve years of teaching.
Barton checks understanding through whole-class simultaneous responses and treats student errors as a flaw in his example sequence, not the learners.
quotes: Whilst this may seem a rather niche example, polygons are an example of what Kris Boulton would call a Category Atom. If you can ask the question: Is this a ___?, and the answer is Yes or No, then you have a Category Atom.
What follows is not an attempt to argue that my approach is better. Instead, it is intended to provide some food for thought.

At this stage, her students are not given any additional guidance—they are free to apply any criteria they like during the sorting process. While this happens, the teacher circulates the room, conversing with students to find out their sorting rules—perhaps some have gone for colour, others for 2D and 3D—and then chooses some students to share their rules with the rest of the class.
Now, I need some data. So, I show my students a selection of other shapes and ask them if each is a polygon. Crucially, I do not call for volunteers or Cold-Call individual students.

If students get an example wrong, I apologise and explain it is my fault for not choosing an appropriate sequence of initial examples. In these cases, I think of a new example on the spot to get us back on track and then improve my initial sequence after the lesson.

Notice that both approaches leave the definition until the very end. Definitions often have little meaning to students, as they are full of abstract concepts of technical vocabulary: A polygon is a plane figure with at least three straight sides and angles.
